title: Tennis Elbow: Causes, Symptoms, and 5 Exercises That Actually Work
excerpt: Tennis elbow isn't just for athletes. Learn what causes lateral epicondylitis, spot symptoms early, and 5 proven exercises to speed up recovery at home.
content:
What Is Tennis Elbow?

Tennis elbow, medically known as lateral epicondylitis, is a painful condition that occurs when the tendons in your elbow become overloaded — usually from repetitive wrist and arm motions. Despite the name, you don't have to play tennis to develop it. In fact, most people who walk into PhysioFix in JP Nagar, Bangalore with tennis elbow have never picked up a racket.

The condition affects the extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle — a small muscle that helps stabilise your wrist when your elbow is straight. When this muscle and its tendon are strained repeatedly, tiny tears develop, leading to inflammation and pain on the outside of the elbow.

Why Tennis Elbow Is So Common in India Today

With the rise of remote work and prolonged screen time, more and more Indians are developing repetitive strain injuries. Activities that commonly trigger tennis elbow include:

  • Desk work: Hours of mouse and keyboard use with poor wrist posture
  • Badminton and cricket: Two of India's most popular sports that involve repetitive arm motion
  • Cooking and household chores: Stirring, chopping, and lifting with improper form
  • Painting or carpentry: Extended gripping and twisting motions
  • Smartphone overuse: Repetitive thumb and wrist strain that radiates to the elbow

What makes this condition particularly tricky is that it often creeps up slowly. You might not feel discomfort during the activity itself — the pain typically shows up hours later or the next morning, making it easy to ignore until it becomes severe.

Key Symptoms to Watch For

Recognising tennis elbow early is the best way to avoid months of discomfort. The hallmark signs include:

Pain on the Outer Elbow

A dull ache or sharp pain on the bony bump on the outside of your elbow (the lateral epicondyle). This is the most common symptom and the one that usually prompts a visit to a physiotherapist.

Weak Grip Strength

You may notice that holding a coffee mug, twisting a doorknob, or even shaking hands feels weaker or painful on the affected side.

Pain That Radiates Down the Forearm

In some cases, the discomfort travels from the elbow down toward the wrist, making everyday tasks like lifting groceries or typing uncomfortable.

Morning Stiffness

If your elbow feels stiff and sore when you wake up but loosens up after moving around, tennis elbow could be the culprit.

5 Exercises to Beat Tennis Elbow

Here are five exercises that consistently deliver results for our patients at PhysioFix. Start gently — if any exercise worsens your pain, scale back the intensity or consult a physiotherapist.

1. Wrist Extensor Stretch

When to do it: Morning and evening, and after any repetitive activity.

  • Extend your affected arm straight in front of you with your palm facing down
  • Use your other hand to gently bend your wrist downward until you feel a stretch on the top of your forearm
  • Hold for 30 seconds
  • Repeat 3 times per session

2. Eccentric Wrist Extension (The Gold Standard)

When to do it: Once daily, after your stretching routine.

  • Rest your forearm on a table with your wrist hanging off the edge, palm facing down
  • Hold a light weight (start with 0.5–1 kg — a water bottle works!) in your hand
  • Use your other hand to lift the weight up (wrist extension)
  • Now, slowly lower the weight down over 4–5 seconds using only your affected wrist
  • Do 3 sets of 10 repetitions

This eccentric exercise is the single most effective movement for repairing the damaged tendon. The controlled lowering phase stimulates collagen production and tendon remodelling.

3. Towel Twist

When to do it: 2–3 times a day, especially before activities that require gripping.

  • Hold a rolled-up towel with both hands, arms extended
  • Twist the towel in opposite directions as if you're wringing out water
  • Hold the twist for 10 seconds, then slowly release
  • Repeat 10 times in each direction

This exercise strengthens your forearm rotator muscles without straining the tendon attachment point.

4. Finger Band Extension

When to do it: As a warm-up before strength exercises.

  • Place a rubber band around your fingers (near the fingertips)
  • Open your fingers against the resistance of the band
  • Hold for 3 seconds, then slowly close
  • Do 3 sets of 15 repetitions

This might seem too simple, but weak finger extensors are almost always part of the tennis elbow picture. Strengthening them reduces the load on the extensor tendons at the elbow.

5. Forearm Pronation and Supination

When to do it: After your eccentric exercise, every other day.

  • Hold a light dumbbell or hammer by one end, with your elbow bent at 90 degrees
  • Slowly rotate your forearm so your palm faces up (supination)
  • Then rotate so your palm faces down (pronation)
  • Move only your forearm — keep your upper arm still
  • Do 3 sets of 12 repetitions on each side

When to See a Physiotherapist

While these exercises can work wonders, some cases of tennis elbow need professional guidance. Consider booking an assessment if:

  • Your pain has persisted for more than 3 weeks despite rest and home exercises
  • You're unable to perform basic daily tasks like lifting a cup or typing
  • The pain wakes you up at night
  • You've noticed numbness or tingling in your fingers (this could indicate nerve involvement)

Prevention: Small Changes, Big Difference

The best treatment is prevention. Here are simple adjustments you can make starting today:

Fix Your Desk Setup

Your mouse and keyboard should be at a height where your elbows rest at a 90-degree angle and your wrists stay straight — not bent up or down. Consider an ergonomic vertical mouse, which keeps your forearm in a neutral position.

Warm Up Before Sports

If you play badminton, tennis, or cricket, spend at least 5 minutes doing arm circles and light wrist stretches before you start. A cold tendon is an injured tendon waiting to happen.

Strengthen Year-Round

Don't wait for pain to start exercising. A consistent routine of forearm and grip strengthening — even twice a week — builds tendon resilience that protects you from injury.

Listen to Your Body

If an activity causes elbow discomfort, stop. Pushing through pain is the fastest route from a mild strain to a chronic condition that takes months to resolve.

Final Thoughts

Tennis elbow can be frustrating — it lingers, affects simple daily tasks, and doesn't always heal quickly on its own. But with the right exercises, proper ergonomics, and professional support when needed, complete recovery is absolutely achievable.
